title: Kindness to animals
hookLine: a man climbs back down a well to bring a thirsty dog water in his shoe
tomorrow: how could God be sick and need a visit?

lines: A MAN, A WELL, A HOT ROAD.
cards: A hot afternoon. A dog tied outside a store, tongue out, no water bowl in sight. People walk past.
Now an older version of that afternoon. A man is walking a hot road, and his thirst gets bad. He finds a well, climbs down, drinks, climbs back up.
And there's a dog, panting, licking the damp ground. The man thinks: this dog is as thirsty as I was. Nobody's watching.
He could walk on. He climbs back down the well.

teach.b: He has no bucket. So he fills his leather shoe with water, holds it in his teeth to free his hands, and climbs up. The dog drinks.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ tells this story in Sahih al-Bukhari, and he ends it this way: God thanked the man for it and forgave him. God thanked him. For a shoe full of water for a stray.
The companions are surprised enough to ask: is there a reward for us even with animals? His answer: in every living creature there is a reward.
The same collection has the reverse story: a woman who shut a cat away and neither fed it nor let it out to find its own food, and she was punished for it. One cat.
The scale runs both ways: a small mercy to an animal weighs a lot, and so does a small cruelty. Then the Qur'an widens the frame.
In Pickthall's words: "There is not an animal in the earth, nor a flying creature flying on two wings, but they are peoples like unto you."

The Arabic word is umam: peoples, communities. The pigeons on the ledge, the ants under the porch, each a community with its own life before God. The line worth repeating tonight: in the Qur'an, animals aren't scenery.

how: Muslims tell the stories of the dog at the well and the woman with the cat to teach mercy to animals; Islamic law on slaughter, working animals and pets draws on the same teaching.

o: keeping a pet clean and well fed at home
eating no meat out of respect for life
mercy toward every creature, wild or tame

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: shut it away with no food

s: in Islam, dogs are outside God's mercy
the Prophet told of a man God thanked and forgave for giving a thirsty dog water.
the Qur'an calls animals and birds peoples like us
6:38: they are peoples like unto you. the Arabic is umam.
kindness to animals is good manners, but the hadith attaches no reward to it
in every living creature there is a reward.

games.q: your little brother pours salt on garden snails to watch them shrivel. 'they're just snails,' he says. what does today's teaching point to?
o: stop him gently; the Qur'an calls creatures peoples, like us.
let it go; snails are pests, and the garden has to come first.
stop him only if Mom is around; it's about manners, not mercy.
games.why: 6:38: no creature on earth but they are peoples like unto you. and the woman with the cat shows a small cruelty weighs too.

practice: Listen for one living sound around you that isn't human: a bird, a dog down the street, an insect, a pet breathing nearby. When you find it, rest your attention there and let it be a whole people with its own life.
If nothing comes, stay with the picture of the dog at the well, drinking.

wordCard.voice: Kindness to animals: mercy toward every creature. In the hadith, a shoe full of water for a thirsty dog earned God's thanks.

orig.note: Arabic: peoples, communities. 6:38 calls animals umam like you; one community is an umma.

carryVoice: Remember this: they are communities too, on two wings or four legs. Bye for now.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2363 (also 2466, 6009; Sahih Muslim 2244): the man, the well and the thirsty dog; God thanked him and forgave him; in every living creature there is a reward
Sahih al-Bukhari 3318 (also Sahih Muslim 2242): the woman who shut a cat away and neither fed it nor let it eat from the earth

sources.q: There is not an animal in the earth, nor a flying creature flying on two wings, but they are peoples like unto you.
